TRANSLATOR'S NOTE

 

Note that in the following translation the numbers 
without brackets refer to the English text, while the numbers in square brackets 
refer to the Greek text. In numbering the lines, the translator has normally 
counted a short indented line with the short line immediately above. The stage

BACKGROUND NOTE

 

Jason was born the son of Aeson, king of Iolcus, a city 
in Thessaly (on the eastern coast of mainland Greece). When his father lost the 
kingship, Jason was secretly sent away and put into the care of the famous 
centaur Chiron, who raised him. As a young man Jason returned to Iolcus. The 
king, Pelias, who had deprived Aeson of the kingship, persuaded Jason to set off 
on an expedition to capture the Golden Fleece, the pure gold skin of a ram, 
which was in a sacred grove in Colchis (a barbarian region to the east of the 
Euxine sea, the Greek name for the Black Sea), where it was guarded by a dragon.

Jason put together a band of adventurers called the Argonauts. They took their 
name from the ship they sailed in, the Argo. The heroes had a number of 
adventures on the way to Colchis. When they arrived in Colchis, king Aeetes set 
Jason a number of tasks, including yoking two fire-breathing bulls, ploughing a 
field with them, sowing the field with the teeth of a dragon, and then fighting 
the warriors who arose from the sown teeth. He also had to confront the dragon 
guarding the fleece.

To complete these tasks Jason enlisted the help of Medea, daughter of king 
Aeetes. She fell in love with Jason and used her magic to help him complete the 
tasks set by Aeetes and to steal the Golden Fleece. She then escaped with Jason, 
killing her brother in order to scatter his body on the sea, so that Aeetes 
would have to hold up his pursuit. Jason and Medea returned to Iolcus, where 
Medea
â
s magic restored Jason
â
s father, Aeson, to youthful health. Medea also 
tricked the daughters of king Pelias into killing their father by giving them 
ineffective medications and persuading them to try a course of treatment which 
was fatal. Because of their culpability in the death of Pelias, Jason and Medea 
were forced to leave Iolchus. They moved to Corinth, where, after a few years, 
Jason decided to leave Medea and marry the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth. 
The story of the play begins immediately after Jasonâs marriage to his new 
bride.

 

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

NURSE: a servant of Medea

TUTOR: a servant assigned to Jasonâs children

MEDEA: wife of Jason

CHORUS: a group of Corinthian women

CREON: king of Corinth

JASON: husband of Medea

AEGEUS: king of Athens

MESSENGER: a servant of Jasonâs

CHILDREN: Medeaâs and Jasonâs two young sons

ATTENDANTS on Creon and Jason.

[Outside the home of Jason and Medea in Corinth. The NURSE, a slave who 
serves Medea, is standing by herself.]

 

NURSE

O how I wish that ship the Argo

had never sailed off to the land of Colchis,

past the Symplegades, those dark dancing rocks

which smash boats sailing through the Hellespont.
(1)

I wish theyâd never chopped the pine trees down

in those mountain forests up on Pelion,

to make oars for the hands of those great men

who set off, on Peliasâs orders,

to fetch the golden fleece.
(2)
 
Then my mistress,

Medea, never would have sailed away                                        

10

to the towers in the land of Iolcus,

her heart passionately in love with Jason.

Sheâd never have convinced those women,

Peliasâ daughters, to kill their father,

and sheâd not have come to live in Corinth                                         
[10]

with her husband and her childrenâwell loved

in exile by those whose land sheâd moved to.

She gave all sorts of help to Jason.

Thatâs when life is most secure and safe,

when woman and her husband stand as one.                            

20

But that marriage changed. Now theyâre enemies.

Their fine loveâs grown sick, diseased, for Jason,

leaving his own children and my mistress, 

is lying on a royal wedding bed.

Heâs married the daughter of king Creon,

who rules this country. As for Medea,

that poor lady, in her disgrace, cries out,                                            
[20]

repeating his oaths, recalling the great trust

in that right hand with which he pledged his love.

She keeps calling to the gods to witness                                     

30

how Jason is repaying her favours.

She just lies there. She wonât eatâher body

she surrenders to the pain, wasting away,

always in tears, ever since she found out

how her husband has dishonoured her.

Sheâs not lifted her eyes up from the ground,

or raised her head. She listens to advice,

even from friends, as if she were a stone,

or the ocean swell, except now and then

she twists that white neck of hers and weeps,                           
40
      
[30]

crying to herself for her dear father, her home,

her own land, all those things she left behind,

to come here with the man who now discards her.

Her suffering has taught her the advantages

of not being cut off from oneâs homeland.

Now she hates her children. When she sees them,

there is no joy in her. And Iâm afraid

she may be up to some new mischief.

Her mind thinks in extremes. I know her well.

Sheâll not put up with being treated badly.                                
50

I worry she may pick up a sharp sword

and stab her stomach, or else sheâll go                                                
[40]

into the house, in silence, to that bed,

and kill the king and bridegroom Jason.

Then sheâll face an even worse disaster.

Sheâs a dangerous woman. It wonât be easy

for any man who picks a fight with her

to think sheâs beaten and heâs triumphed.

 

[Enter Medeaâs and Jasonâs CHILDREN with their 
TUTOR.]

 

Here come her children. Theyâve finished playing.

Theyâve no notion of their motherâs troubles.                            

60

Young minds donât like to dwell on pain.

 

TUTOR

Old slave from my mistressâs household,

why are you here, standing by the gate,                                              
[50]

all alone, complaining to yourself

about whatâs wrong? How come Medea

is willing to stay inside without you?

 

NURSE

Old servant of Jasonâs children,

when a masterâs lot falls out badly,

thatâs bad for faithful servants, tooâ

it affects their hearts as well. My sorrow                                    

70

was so great, I wanted to come here,

to speak to earth and heaven, to tell them

about the wrongs inflicted on my mistress.

 

TUTOR

Unhappy lady! Has she stopped weeping yet?

 

NURSE

Stopped crying? I envy your ignorance.                                               
[60]

Her suffering has only just begunâ

sheâs not even half way through it.

 

TUTOR

                                                          
Poor foolâ

if I can speak that way about my masters.

She knows nothing of her latest troubles.

 

NURSE

Whatâs that, old man? Donât spare me the news.                     

80

 

TUTOR

Nothing. Iâm sorry I said anything.

 

NURSE

Come on, donât hide it from a fellow slave.

I can keep quiet if I have to.

 

TUTOR

Well, I was passing by those benches

where the old men gamble by Peirene,

at the holy spring, and I heard someone say

(I was pretending I wasnât listening)

that Creon, king of this country, intends

to ship the children away from Corinth,                                              

[70]

with their mother, too. Iâve no idea                                             
90

if the storyâs true or not. I hope itâs not.

 

NURSE

But surely Jason wouldnât let his children

go into exile, even if heâs squabbling

with their mother?

 

TUTOR

                          
Old devotions fade,

pushed aside by new relationships.

Jason is no friend of people in this house.

 

NURSE

If we must add these brand-new troubles

to our old ones, before weâve dealt with them,

then weâre finished.

 

TUTOR

But listenâthe timeâs not right                                                  

100
     

[80]

to let your mistress know about these things.

So keep quiet. Donât mention anything.

 

NURSE

Children, do you hear what sort of man

your father is to you? My curse on him!

No. He is my masterâbut a bad man

to his own family. Of that heâs guilty.

 

TUTOR

What mortal man is not? Donât you know yet

all men love themselves more than their neighbours.

And some are right to do thatâwhile others

just want some benefit. But this father,                                      

110

with his new wife, has no love for his children.

 

NURSE

Come on, children, get inside the house.

Things will be fine.

 

[To the TUTOR]

 

                       
You must keep them awayâ                                         
[90]

as far as possibleâand donât bring them

near their mother when sheâs in this state.

Iâve seen her look at them with savage eyes,

as if she means to injure them somehow.

I know this anger of hers will not end,

not before she turns it loose on someone.

I hope it falls on enemies, not friends!                                  

120

 

MEDEA 
 

[crying from inside the house]

I canât stand this pain, this misery.

What do I do? I wish that I could die!

 

NURSE

My dear children, you hear your motherâs cry.

Her heartâs upset. Her angerâs growing, too.

So quickly now, run off inside the house.                                           
[100]

Stay out of sight. Donât try to go and see her.

Sheâs fierce, headstrong by nature. Take care.

So go nowâinside as quickly as you can.

 

[The TUTOR and CHILDREN enter the house.]

 

Itâs obvious the cloud of bitter grief

rising in her is only just the start.                                         
130

As her temper grows even more intense,

it will soon catch fire. Sheâs a passionate soul,

hard to restrain. What will she do next,

now her heartâs been bitten by these injuries?                                   

[110]

 

MEDEA 
 

[from inside the house]

The pain of this sufferingâthis intense pain.

Am I not right to weep? O my children,

cursed children of a hateful motherâ

may you die with your father and his house,

may it all perish, crash down in ruins!

 

NURSE

O the sorrow of it all. Poor woman!                                            

140

Why link your children with the nasty things

their fatherâs done? Why do you hate them so?

Iâm terrified the children will be hurt.

The pride of rulers is something to fearâ

they often order men, but seldom listen,                                            
[120]

and when their tempers change itâs hard to bear.

Itâs better to get used to living life

as an equal common person. Anyway,

I donât want a grand life for myselfâ

just to grow old with some security.                                           
150

They say a moderate lifeâs the best of all,

a far better choice for mortal men.

Going for too much brings no benefits.

And when the gods get angry with some home,

the more wealth it has, the more it is destroyed.                                
[130]

 

[Enter the CHORUS of Corinthian women.]

 

CHORUS LEADER

I heard her voice, I heard the cries

of that sad lady here from Colchis.

Has she not calmed down yet? Old nurse, tell me.

I heard from some household servant in there

that sheâs been screaming. I find no pleasure                            

160

in this houseâs suffering. Weâve been friends.

 

NURSE

This house is finishedâalready ruined.

For Jasonâs bound by his new marriage tie                                          
[140]

to the kingâs daughter. As for my mistress,

her tears are washing away her life in there,

inside the house. She finds no consolation

in the words of any of her friends.

 

MEDEA 
 

[still from inside the house]

O why canât a bolt of lightning strike me?

What point is there in living anymore?

I want death to come and sweep me off!                                    
170

Let me escape this life of suffering!

 

CHORUS

O Zeus and Earth and Sunâ

do you hear how this young wife

sings out her misery?                                                                           

[150]

Thoughtless lady,

why long for deathâs marriage bed

which human beings all shun?

Death comes soon enough

and brings an end to everything.

You should not pray for it.                                                          

180

And if your husband

devotes himself to some new bed,

why get angry over that?

Zeus will plead for you in this.

Donât waste your life away,

with too much wailing for your husband.

 

MEDEA 
 

[within]

O great Themis and noble Artemis,                                                    

[160]

do you see what I am having to endure,

when Iâm the one who bound that cursed man,

my husband, with strong promises to me?                                 
190

O how I want to see him and his bride

beaten down, destroyedâtheir whole house as wellâ

for these wrongs they dare inflict on me,

when Iâve done nothing to provoke them!

O father and city, I left you behind

in my disgrace when I killed my brother.
(3)

 

NURSE

Do you hear whatâs sheâs saying, how she calls

to Themis, who hears our prayers, and Zeus,

who guards, they say, the promises men swear.                                 
[170]

Sheâs bound to do something quite serious                               

200

before this rage of hers comes to an end.

 

CHORUS LEADER

I wish sheâd let us see her face to face

and listen to what we have to tell her.

That might calm down her savage temper,

the fury in her heart. Iâd like the chance

to show good will to a lady whom I like.

Go nowâbring her here outside the house.                                       
[180]

Tell her sheâll be among some friends of hers.

And hurry, before she harms someone in thereâ

that power in her grief will make her act.                                   
210

 

NURSE

All right, though Iâm afraid I wonât persuade

my mistress. Still, as a favour to you,

Iâll see what I can do. Right now she glares

at servants when they come close to her

to tell her something. Sheâs just like a bull

or lioness with cubsâthatâs how she looks.

Those men from long agoâyouâd not be wrong                                 
[190]

to call them fools without much wisdom.

They thought up songs for celebrations,

feasts and banquets, bringing to human life                              
220

delightful music. But they found nothing

in music or the lyreâs many strings

to end the bitterness of human life,

the pain in living, sorrows bringing on

deaths and horrifying calamities

that destroy whole families. What a blessing

it would be for human beings if music

could cure these sorrows. When people feast,                                    
[200]

why should people sing? Itâs a waste of time.

People who eat well are happy anywayâ                                   
230

theyâve enjoyed the pleasure of the meal.

 

[NURSE exits into the house.]

 

CHORUS

I have heard Medeaâs crying,

full of sorrow, full of tears,

her shrill accusations against Jason,

the husband whoâs betrayed her.

Suffering such injustice, she cries out,

calling the godsâcalling Themis,

Zeusâs daughter, goddess of those promises

which carried her across the ocean

to Hellas, through the black salt waves,                                     
240
     
[210]

through the place which few men penetrate,

that strait which guards the Pontic Sea.

 

[Enter MEDEA with the NURSE.]

 

MEDEA

Women of Corinth, I have come 
out here,

outside the house, so you wonât think ill of me.

Many men, I know, become too arrogant,

both in the public eye and in their homes.

Others get a reputation for indifference,

because they stay at ease within the house.

Thereâs no justice in the eyes of mortal men.

Before they know someoneâs deep character,                             
250
     

[220]

they hate the sight of her, though sheâs not hurt them.

A guest of the city must comply, of course,

act as the city wants. I donât commend

a stubborn man, not even a citizen,

who thanks to his stupidity annoys

his fellow townsmen. But in my case,

this unexpected blow thatâs hit me

has destroyed my heart. My life is over,

dear friends. Iâve lost all joy. I want to die.

The person who was everything to me,                                      
260

my own husband, has turned out to be

the worst of men. This I know is true.

Of all things with life and understanding,                                          
[230]

we women are the most unfortunate.

First, we need a husband, someone we get

for an excessive price. He then becomes

the ruler of our bodies. And this misfortune

adds still more troubles to the grief we have.

Then comes the crucial struggle: this husband

we have selected, is he good or bad?                                          
270

For a divorce loses women all respect,

yet we canât refuse to take a husband.

Then, when she goes into her husbandâs home,

with its new rules and different customs,

she needs a prophetâs skill to sort out the man

whose bed she shares. She canât learn that at home.                          

[240]

Once weâve worked hard at this, and with success,

our husband accepts the marriage yoke

and lives in peaceâan enviable life.

But if the marriage doesnât work, then death                             
280

is much to be preferred. When the man tires

of the company he keeps at home, he leaves,

seeking relief for his distress elsewhere,

outside the home. He gets his satisfaction

with some male friend or someone his own age.

We women have to look at just one man.

Men tell us we live safe and secure at home,

while they must go to battle with their spears.

How stupid they are! Iâd rather stand there

three times in battle holding up my shield                                 
290
    

[250]

than give birth once. But your story and mine

are not the same. For you have a city,

you have your fatherâs house, enjoy your life

with friends for company. But Iâm alone.

I have no city, and Iâm being abused

by my own husband. I was carried off,

a trophy from a barbarian land.

I have no mother, brother, or relation

to shelter with in this extremity.

And so I want to ask something from you.                                 
300

If I find some way to punish Jason                                                       
[260]

for these injusticesâhis bride, as well,

and her fatherâsay nothing. In other things

a woman may be timidâin watching battles

or seeing steel, but when sheâs hurt in love,

her marriage violated, thereâs no heart

more desperate for blood than hers.

 

CHORUS LEADER

Iâll do what you request. For you are right

to pay back your husband. And, Medea,

Iâm not surprised you grieve at these events.                             

310

 

[Enter Creon, with armed attendants.]

 

I see Creon, king of Corinth, coming.

Heâll be bringing news, announcing

some new decision thatâs been made.                                                 
[270]

 

CREON

You there, Medea, scowling in anger

against your husband. Iâm ordering you

out of Corinth. You must go into exile,

and take those two children of yours with you.

Go quickly. Iâm here to make quite sure

that this decree is put into effect.

Iâm not going back into the palace                                              
320

until Iâve cast you out beyond our borders.

 

MEDEA

O now my sufferings will kill me. Itâs over.

My enemies have set full sail against me,

and thereâs no way I can avert disaster.

But, Creon, let me ask you somethingâ                                             
[280]

since Iâm the one abused, why banish me?

What have I done?

 

CREON

                                                       
I am afraid of you.

I wonât conceal the truth. Thereâs a good chance

you might well instigate some fatal harm

against my daughter. Many things lead me                                
330

to this conclusion: youâre a clever woman,

very experienced in evil ways;

youâre grieving the loss of your husbandâs bed;

and from reports I hear youâre making threats

to take revenge on Jason, on his bride,

and on her father. Before that happens,

Iâm taking some precautions. Woman,                                                
[290]

itâs better that you hate me than for me

to grow soft now and regret it later.

 

MEDEA

Alas, this is not the first time, Creon,                                          

340

my reputation has badly damaged me.

Itâs happened often. No man with any sense

should ever educate his children

to know anything beyond whatâs normal.

Quite apart from charges of idleness

which other people bring against them,

they stir up in their fellow citizens

a hostile envy. If you offer fools

some brand new wisdom, theyâll consider you

quite useless, not someone wise. And if,                                    

350
    
[300]

within the city, people think of you

as greater than those men who seem quite wise,

youâll be a nuisance. So it is with me.

Iâm a knowledgeable woman. I make

some people envious. Others say Iâm shy.

Some the opposite. Some say Iâm hostile.

Iâm not that clever, but still you fear me.

Have I hurt you at all, made you suffer?

Donât fear me, Creon. Itâs not in me

to commit crimes against the men in charge.                            

360

Besides, in what way have you injured me?

Youv have married your daughter to a man,

one your heart selected. My husbandâs                                               
[310]

the one I hate. In my view, youâve acted

in this business with good sense. So now,

Iâll not begrudge you your prosperity.

Have your marriage, and good luck to you.

But let me remain here, in this country.

Although Iâve suffered an injustice,

Iâll obey the rulers and stay silent.                                               

370

 

CREON

What you say sounds comforting enough,

but Iâm still afraid that heart of yours

is planning something evil. At this point,

I trust you even less than previously.

Passionate people, women as well as men,

are easier to protect oneself against,                                                    
[320]

than someone clever who keeps silent.

No. You must leave Corinthâand right away.

No more speeches. I have made up my mind.

Itâs not possible for you to stay here,                                           

380

not with us, given your hostility to me.

 

MEDEA 
 

[kneeling in front of Creon]

No, donât send me away. Iâm begging you,

at your knee, in your daughterâs name.

 

CREON

Your words are useless. You wonât persuade me.

 

MEDEA

Youâll send me into exile without hearing

my supplication?

 

CREON

                                                     
Indeed I will.

I donât love you more than my own family.

 

MEDEA

O my homeland! How Iâm thinking of you now.

 

CREON

Except for my own children, my country

is what I cherish most by far.

 

MEDEA

                                                            
Alas,                                  
390

loveâs a miserable thing for mortal men.                                             
 [330]

 

CREON

I think events determine if thatâs true.

 

MEDEA

O Zeus, donât overlook who bears the blame

for all this evil.

 

CREON

                                       
Itâs time to leave,

you foolish woman. Time to rid myself

of all this trouble.

 

MEDEA

                                   
We have trouble enoughâ

Thereâs no need for any more.

 

CREON

                                                     
Come onâ

or my servants will force you into exile.

 

MEDEA

No, donât do that. I beg you, Creon . . .

 

[Medea seizes Creonâs hand.]

 

CREON

Woman, it seems youâre trying to provoke me.                        

  400

 

MEDEA

All right then. I will go into exile.

I wasnât begging to escape from that.

 

CREON

Then why squeeze my hand so hard and not let go?

 

MEDEA

Let me remain here one day to prepare,                                             
 [340]

to get ready for my exile and provide

something for my children, since their father,

as one more insult, does nothing for them.

Have pity on them. Youâre a parent, too.

You should treat them kindlyâthatâs whatâs right.

If I go into exile, I donât care,                                                      
  410

but I weep for them in their misfortune.

 

CREON

For a tyrant my will is by nature tender,

and by feeling pity Iâve been hurt before,

more than once. And now, woman, I see

Iâm making a mistake, for you can have                                              
 [350]

your extra day. But let me warn youâ

if the sun catches you tomorrow

within the borders of this country,

you or your children, youâll be put to death.

Donât assume Iâm not telling you the truth.                              
  420

So, if you must remain, stay one more day.

In that time you canât do the harm I fear.

 

[Exit Creon with his attendants.]

 

CHORUS LEADER

Alas for you, unfortunate womanâ

how wretched your distress. Where will you turn?

Where will you find someone to take you in?

What country, what home will you ever find

to save you from misfortune?                                                              

[360]

 

MEDEA

Things have worked out badly in every way.

Who can deny the fact? But nonetheless,

you should not assume thatâs how things will stay.                  
 430

The newly wedded pair still face some struggles,

and the man who made this marriage happen

might have serious problems yet. Do you think

Iâd prostrate myself before a man like that,

if there was no advantage to be gained?

If I did not have some plan in mind,

Iâd not have talked to him or grabbed his hand.
